chunks: What Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn, from Hammad ibn 'Isa and Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said:

I asked him about a man who had designated a sacrificial offering while it was fat, then illness afflicted it and its eye burst or it became broken, yet it reached the place of sacrifice while still alive. He said: He should slaughter it, and it has sufficed for him. And it is possible that what is meant by this is one who is not able to provide a substitute, because one whose condition is such is excused; but as for when one has the ability, then a substitute is unavoidable. This is indicated by that.

key_terms.أَجْزَأَ عَنْهُ: it sufficed and fulfilled his obligation
key_terms.الْبَدَلِ: a substitute animal replacing the defective one
key_terms.الْمَنْحَرَ: the place of slaughter for the sacrificial offering
key_terms.انْفَقَأَتْ عَيْنُهُ: its eye became ruptured, indicating a serious defect
key_terms.سَمِينٌ: fat and sound in condition at the time of selection
key_terms.مَرَضٌ: an illness that affects the sacrificial animal
key_terms.هَدْيًا: a sacrificial offering designated for hajj rites

ai.seo_question: If a hajj sacrificial animal becomes defective before reaching the place of slaughter, does it still suffice?
ai.summary: This hadith addresses the ruling of a sacrificial animal for hajj when it develops a defect after having been selected in sound condition but still reaches the place of slaughter alive. The Imam عليه السلام states that it may be slaughtered and suffice, while the appended wording clarifies that this may apply to one unable to replace it; if replacement is possible, a substitute is required.
